title: Budget GPUs Face Deepening Shortage as AI Demand Devours Memory Supply
excerpt: Zotac warns the situation is "serious enough to raise concerns about the very survival of graphics card manufacturers," as Nvidia reportedly shelves new consumer GPU launches for the first time in decades.
body:
• Zotac Korea warned that memory shortages and "unreasonable" pricing from Nvidia threaten the survival of graphics card manufacturers and distributors
  • Nvidia has reportedly canceled the RTX 50 Super refresh and delayed the next-gen RTX 60 series, marking the first year in three decades without a new consumer GPU launch
  • AI data center demand is consuming memory supply, with AI chips carrying 65% profit margins versus 40% for gaming GPUs — making consumer cards a lower priority
  • Production of RTX 50-series cards could be cut 30-40% compared to early 2025, with 16GB mid-range models like the RTX 5070 Ti and 5060 Ti hit hardest

The consumer graphics card market is heading into its worst supply crunch since the crypto-mining era, and this time the culprit is artificial intelligence. Zotac, one of Nvidia's largest add-in board partners, issued a stark warning from its Korean division: the current situation is "extremely serious — serious enough to raise concerns about the very survival of graphics card manufacturers and distributors going forward."

A Manufacturer's Alarm Bell

The Zotac Korea statement, posted on the company's official TagTag Mall storefront in late January and translated by hardware leaker @harukaze5719, laid out the problem in blunt terms. Memory supply is not coming in. GPU supply volumes are being reduced. Several GeForce RTX 50-series models will be unavailable for an "extended period of time." The latest pricing from Nvidia is "unreasonable" — affecting not just the flagship RTX 5090 but also the mainstream RTX 5060.

https://x.com/MilkRoadAI/status/2089056707704127963

Zotac expressed particular concern about GPUs not manufactured using Samsung's processes, suggesting that stable supply of cards built on TSMC's nodes may no longer be feasible. The company temporarily slashed reward points to 0% in an effort to keep retail pricing as low as possible.

"Not only has the price of the RTX 5090 increased sharply, but the price hike for the 5060 is also substantial."

— Zotac Korea, official notice to customers

Why AI Is Eating the GPU Market

The root cause is a global memory shortage driven by AI infrastructure spending. Memory manufacturers have shifted production capacity toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and other components for AI workloads, driving up prices for consumer-oriented GDDR and DDR chips. Nvidia's AI accelerators use massive amounts of the same memory that goes into gaming cards, and the company is prioritizing the more profitable segment.

The economics are stark. According to The Information, Nvidia's AI chips carry profit margins of approximately 65%, compared to 40% for consumer graphics cards. Gaming GPU revenue has shrunk from 35% of Nvidia's total in the first nine months of 2022 to roughly 8% in the same period of 2025. When memory is scarce, the allocation decision makes itself.

No New Consumer GPUs This Year

The supply squeeze has already reshaped Nvidia's product roadmap. The company has reportedly canceled or postponed the planned RTX 50 Super refresh — traditionally a mid-year update — and pushed back the next-generation RTX 60 series beyond its originally planned 2027 mass production timeline. If confirmed, 2026 would be the first year in roughly three decades that Nvidia has not launched a new consumer GPU.

Production of existing RTX 50-series cards could be cut by 30% to 40% compared to the first half of 2025, according to reports citing industry insiders. Mid-range models with 16GB of GDDR7 — the RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5060 Ti — are expected to be hit hardest, precisely the cards that mainstream gamers need most as 8GB VRAM becomes insufficient for modern titles.

"The current situation is so serious that it raises concerns about whether graphics card manufacturers and distributors can continue to operate."

— Zotac Korea, translated statement

The RTX 3060 Comeback

In a sign of how desperate the supply picture has become, Nvidia is reportedly preparing to resume production of the GeForce RTX 3060 — a budget card from the Ampere generation that was previously discontinued. The RTX 3060 uses older Samsung-manufactured memory that is not competing with AI demand, making it one of the few cards that can still be produced affordably. It remains one of the most popular GPUs in use, according to Steam's hardware surveys.

For PC gamers, the message is clear: premium cards will cost more, mid-range cards may be unavailable for months, and the traditional upgrade cycle has been broken by AI's insatiable appetite for silicon and memory. Whether this is a temporary squeeze or a permanent reordering of Nvidia's priorities will depend on how long the AI infrastructure boom lasts — and whether memory manufacturers can expand capacity fast enough to serve both markets.
